how.lead: Only the two ends are fixed. The seven values between were chosen by reasoning from guidance on wet electrical equipment, so that the transformer is damaged more gradually than switchgear. No measured outcome sits behind them.

steps.t: Where it starts: no water, no damage
steps.d: Depth is measured at the part itself, so below the part’s lowest critical point the damage is zero.

steps.t: Why the first centimetres already count
steps.d: Water entering a control section, a cable entry or a low vent can trigger replacement or evaluation before deep submersion. So the table has values at 2 cm and 5 cm.

steps.t: Why it is gentler than switchgear
steps.d: The cell reads NEMA’s guidance as treating liquid-filled transformers differently: the fluid can be analysed and the unit evaluated, not always replaced. So at every depth the transformer’s value sits below the switchgear’s. NEMA GD 1-2019’s own table lists liquid-filled transformers under Replace, with fluid analysis required to evaluate, so this reading is worth a check.
refs: NEMA GD 1-2019, Evaluating Water-Damaged Electrical Equipment, p. 4

steps.t: Why a table of depths, and not a smooth curve
steps.d: Flood guidance is threshold-like: water is in the equipment, or it is not. The US Army Corps’ HEC-FIA depth tables are the precedent for writing damage as a table of depths joined by straight lines. Only the form is taken, none of the values.
